newsitem.title: INDIA: Italy's Snamprogetti denies link to Bofors affair.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Snamprogetti denies link to Bofors affair.

text.p: Italian engineering firm Snamprogetti Spa on Friday denied any involvement in alleged payments by Swedish arms manufacturer Bofors AB connected with a $1.3 billion Indian artillery contract in 1986.
In a front-page advertisement in the Times of India newspaper, Snamprogetti denied involvement and said "recent press reports concerning the 'Bofors case' could damage the company's image".

On Tuesday, Indian investigators released the names of five people -- including a former Snamprognetti official -- they said had received money in connection with the contract, which governed the sale of Bofors field artillery guns to the Indian government.
The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) said documents obtained from Swiss authorities revealed that the five people had received the payments from Bofors, a unit of Swedish defence group Celsius.
The CBI said Ottavio Quattrocchi, the Indian representative of Snamprogetti when the contract was signed, and his wife Maria were among the five.
"Snamprogetti has nothing to do with the matter under investigation," the Italian firm said in the advertisement.
"The present company representative in India appointed in January 1994, in accordance with Snamprogetti's policy, has already cooperated with CBI," it said.
A Snamprogetti executive in New Delhi confirmed that the firm had placed the advertisement and said the current company representative was Enrico Stacul.
Quattrocchi released a statement in Kuala Lumpur on Friday denying he had ever had any relationship with Bofors.
Swiss police have said there was evidence Bofors paid about $40 million into various banks accounts in Switzerland during the time the contract with India was drawn up and settled.

Bofors said on Wednesday that it saw no need to reopen the investigation into the contract. A Bofors spokeswoman in Stockholm said the firm had paid money as final payments to its agents, not as bribes.
The furore over the alleged payments contributed to the defeat in 1989 of the government of late prime minister Rajiv Gandhi, who was accused of involvement in the affair.
Gandhi, who denied the allegations, was assassinated while campaigning for 1991 parliamentary polls.
